The Famine Stela on Sehel Island records a seven-year famine ended when Djoser restored Khnum's temple, a text carved in the Ptolemaic period but claiming Old Kingdom authority.
entities.variantTraditions: The Famine Stela is a Ptolemaic composition asserting an ancient land grant to the priesthood, not a contemporary Third Dynasty record.

entities.name: Wadjet
entities.role: Cobra goddess of Lower Egypt
domains: the uraeus that spits fire at enemies
entities.bio: The cobra who rears on the king's brow, patron of Lower Egypt and half of the Two Ladies.
entities.longBio: Wadjet is the uraeus, the rearing cobra worn at the front of the royal headdress, and her function is direct: she spits fire at whoever approaches the king with harm in mind. As patron of Lower Egypt she pairs with Nekhbet the vulture of Upper Egypt to form the Two Ladies, one of the five great titles of every pharaoh and the clearest statement of the unified kingdom in the royal titulary. She is counted among the forms of the Eye of Ra, which is what gives her the fire. In the Osiris story she is one of those who shelter Isis and the infant Horus in the marshes of Chemmis. Her name means the green one, from the papyrus that grew across her Delta homeland.
entities.variantTraditions: The wedjat eye of Horus and the goddess Wadjet are etymologically related and often conflated in amulet contexts, though they are distinct.

entities.name: Nekhbet
entities.role: Vulture goddess of Upper Egypt
symbols: the shen ring in her talons
entities.bio: The vulture of Upper Egypt, who with Wadjet forms the Two Ladies of the royal titulary.
entities.longBio: Nekhbet spreads her wings above the king in protection, often shown hovering over the throne clutching the shen ring of eternity. As patron of Upper Egypt she is the southern half of the Two Ladies, and the vulture and cobra heads appear side by side on the royal brow when both kingdoms are meant. Her association with vultures gave her a maternal character rather than a grim one, since Egyptians observed the bird's attentive care of its young, and she is called mother of mothers and shown as a nurse to the king. The vulture headdress worn by queens is hers. Her city Nekheb sits opposite Nekhen, Hierakonpolis, one of the oldest centres of kingship in Egypt, which explains her closeness to the throne.
entities.variantTraditions: The Greeks identified her with Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth, and called her city Eileithyiaspolis.

entities.name: Serqet
entities.role: Scorpion goddess of venom and breathing
epithets: She Who Causes the Throat to Breathe
entities.bio: Goddess of venomous stings, who both causes and cures them, and one of the four canopic guardians.
entities.longBio: Serqet's name means she who causes the throat to breathe, which reads either as a description of what she does for the healed or of the constriction she inflicts, and Egyptian religion is comfortable with both meanings at once: the power over venom is the power to withhold it. Her priests were practising physicians and magicians who treated scorpion stings, a serious hazard in a country where scorpions are common. She is one of the four goddesses - with Isis, Nephthys and Neith - who guard the canopic jars and the corners of the sarcophagus, and she watches over Qebehsenuef. She also appears among the goddesses who protect Isis and the infant Horus in the marshes, sending seven scorpions to accompany them.
entities.variantTraditions: Her scorpion is usually shown without its sting and claws, apparently to render the image safe to have nearby.

entities.name: Hapi
entities.role: God of the inundation
domains: the fertility of the black land
symbols: a heavy blue-green body with pendulous breasts
entities.abode: The caverns at the cataract from which the flood was believed to issue
entities.bio: The inundation personified: a well-fed figure with heavy breasts and a swollen belly, bringing abundance.
entities.longBio: Hapi is not the Nile itself but the flood - the annual rise that laid new silt across the fields and decided whether Egypt would eat. He is shown as a man with blue or green skin, a swollen belly and heavy breasts, because he nourishes, and the androgyny is deliberate rather than accidental. In scenes of the union of the Two Lands, two Hapi figures tie the papyrus and lotus together around the sema sign, binding Upper and Lower Egypt with the river that runs through both. He had no great temple, being honoured instead at the cataract and by offerings thrown into the water as the flood began, and hymns to him survive in numbers that reflect how much depended on him. His exact source was unknown and was said to lie in caverns guarded by Khnum.
entities.variantTraditions: Hapi shares his name with one of the four sons of Horus, who is a different figure entirely.

entities.name: Wepwawet
entities.role: Opener of the ways
domains: leading the dead into the underworld
symbols: the standing grey jackal or wolf
entities.bio: A jackal god who goes ahead: before the army, before the king, and before the dead.
entities.longBio: Wepwawet's name is a job description - opener of the ways - and it applies at every scale. His standard was carried in front of the king in procession and at the head of the army, clearing the road. In the funerary sphere he opens the way into the underworld for the dead, and his image presides over the Opening of the Mouth ceremony that restored the mummy's senses. At Abydos he led the great procession of Osiris. He is easily confused with Anubis, being also canine, but he is usually shown standing rather than couchant and coloured grey or white rather than black, and Greek visitors called his city Lycopolis, wolf-city, because they took him for a wolf.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Wepwawet is a jackal or a wolf was already unclear in antiquity; the two were sometimes treated as one god with Anubis and sometimes kept separate.

entities.name: Sokar
entities.role: Falcon god of the Memphite necropolis
domains: the dark hours of the underworld
symbols: the falcon head on a mummiform body
festivals: The Festival of Sokar, with the henu barque dragged in procession
entities.bio: Hawk-headed lord of the Memphite cemetery and of the deepest hours of the night journey.
entities.longBio: Sokar governs the necropolis at Saqqara, which takes its name from him, and the region called Rosetau, understood as the entrance to the underworld passages. In the Book of the Underworld he presides over the fourth and fifth hours of the night, the darkest and most difficult stretch of the sun's journey, a sandy region the barque must be dragged through rather than sailed. He is a god of the dead but also, through his Memphite association with Ptah, a patron of metalworking. Fused into the composite Ptah-Sokar-Osiris, he appears in enormous numbers of small painted wooden statues placed in tombs of the Late Period. His festival involved dragging his henu barque, a boat mounted on a sledge, around the walls.
entities.variantTraditions: The three-part fusion Ptah-Sokar-Osiris merges creator, necropolis and resurrection into one funerary figure and is late; the three were originally distinct.

entities.name: Nefertum
entities.role: The lotus at the sun's first rising
epithets: The Lotus at the Nose of Ra
entities.bio: The blue lotus from which the sun first rose, and god of perfume.
entities.longBio: One creation account has the newborn sun rise from a blue lotus floating on the primeval waters, and Nefertum is that lotus. He completes the Memphite triad as the son of Ptah and Sekhmet, and is shown as a youth with a lotus blossom on his head, often flanked by two tall plumes. Because the blue lotus is intensely fragrant and opens at dawn to close at dusk, he is also the god of perfume and of the scented unguents Egyptians used heavily, and one text calls him the lotus at the nose of Ra - the flower the sun god holds to breathe. His character is gentle and his mother's is not, which is a pairing the Memphite theology seems to have found productive rather than contradictory.
entities.variantTraditions: In some accounts his mother is Bastet or Wadjet rather than Sekhmet, following whichever local goddess was Ptah's consort.

entities.name: Heqet
entities.role: Frog goddess of birth
entities.bio: Frog-headed midwife of the gods, who breathes life into the body Khnum has shaped.
entities.longBio: Egyptians watched the Nile fill with frogs as the inundation receded and read the animal as a sign of abundant new life, so the goddess of the last stage of birth is a frog. Heqet works alongside Khnum: he moulds the child on his wheel, and she gives it life and hastens the delivery. In the Westcar Papyrus she and a group of goddesses disguise themselves as travelling musicians to attend the birth of three future kings, which is one of the very few Egyptian narratives to show a birth in domestic detail. Amulets and wands carrying her image were used by women in labour, and her name appears on ivory knives meant to cut a protective circle around the birthing bed.
entities.variantTraditions: The much later Coptic association of the frog with resurrection may or may not descend from Heqet; the connection is asserted more often than demonstrated.

entities.name: Meskhenet
entities.role: Goddess of the birthing brick and of destiny
symbols: the birth brick with a human head
a headdress of two curled cow's uterus symbols
entities.abode: At the birthing bricks, and at the judgment
entities.bio: The brick Egyptian women squatted on to give birth, personified, who speaks each child's destiny.
entities.longBio: Egyptian women gave birth crouched on a pair of mud bricks, and Meskhenet is that brick made a goddess, shown either as a brick with a woman's head or as a woman wearing a curious two-pronged emblem. Her role goes beyond assisting: she declares the child's fate at the moment of birth, so that the shape of a life is spoken over it at the beginning. In the Westcar Papyrus she attends the births of the three kings and announces the kingship of each as it is born. She reappears at the other end of life, standing near the scales at the judgment, where she can testify to what the person was allotted - a neat closing of the circle, since the goddess who spoke the destiny is present when it is assessed.
entities.variantTraditions: Meskhenet is sometimes multiplied into four goddesses, one for each of the bricks or for each stage of the birth.

entities.name: Renenutet
entities.role: Cobra goddess of the harvest and of nursing
symbols: the cobra-headed woman nursing a child
entities.abode: The threshing floor and the granary
festivals: A harvest festival at the threshing floor, giving her name to the month Pharmuthi
entities.bio: The cobra of the harvest, who guards the granary and nurses the newborn.
entities.longBio: Snakes gathered in Egyptian granaries and threshing floors hunting rodents, and Renenutet is that observed fact turned into the goddess who protects the stored grain. Her festival fell at harvest, when offerings were made at the threshing floor, and her image guarded granaries and wine presses. Her second domain follows from the first: she nourishes, and so she suckles infants and is present at the giving of a name, which in Egyptian thought is part of what makes a person real. She is sometimes given as the mother of Nehebkau, and in a funerary context she can appear as the linen bandages that wrap the mummy. The month of Pharmuthi, and modern Coptic Parmoute, carries her name.
entities.variantTraditions: Her name is variously rendered Renenutet, Ernutet or Thermuthis; the Greeks identified her with Isis in her harvest aspect.

entities.name: Nehebkau
entities.role: Serpent who joins the ka to the body
domains: the binding of the ka to the body
symbols: a serpent with human arms and legs
entities.bio: A two-headed serpent who binds the ka to the body after death, making continued existence possible.
entities.longBio: Nehebkau begins as a hostile serpent of the underworld and is subdued - in one text Atum presses a fingernail to his spine - after which he becomes a servant of order rather than a threat. His name means he who harnesses or yokes the kas, and his function is precise and important: at death the ka, the vital essence, separates from the body, and Nehebkau reunites them so that the person can continue to exist. Without that joining the elaborate machinery of the tomb accomplishes nothing. He is also invoked against snakebite and scorpion venom, on the principle that the greatest serpent can restrain the lesser ones. In some texts he is a son of Renenutet, and in others he is counted among the assessors at the judgment.
entities.variantTraditions: His transformation from adversary to servant is not narrated so much as assumed; different texts treat him as either without reconciling them.

entities.name: The Four Sons of Horus
entities.role: Guardians of the organs of the dead
symbols: the four canopic jar stoppers: human, baboon, jackal and falcon
entities.abode: The canopic chest, beside the coffin
entities.bio: Four brothers who guard the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, each with a goddess behind him.
entities.longBio: When a body was embalmed the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines were removed, dried, wrapped and placed in four jars, and each organ was assigned to one of the Four Sons of Horus, each of whom was in turn protected by one of the four goddesses. Imsety, human-headed, took the liver with Isis; Hapi, baboon-headed, the lungs with Nephthys; Duamutef, jackal-headed, the stomach with Neith; Qebehsenuef, falcon-headed, the intestines with Serqet. They are also aligned with the four cardinal points, which places the dead body at the centre of an ordered space. In earlier practice all four jar stoppers were human heads; the distinctive animal heads appear from the New Kingdom onward. The heart was deliberately left in the body, since it was needed for the weighing.
entities.variantTraditions: The Hapi of the canopic jars is a different god from Hapi of the inundation, sharing only the name.

entities.name: Aker
entities.role: The double lion of the horizon
domains: the horizon at both ends of the night
the guarding of the sun's passage
symbols: two lions or two human heads back to back
the strip of land between them
entities.abode: The eastern and western horizons at once
entities.bio: Two lions sitting back to back, the western and eastern gates the sun passes between each night.
entities.longBio: Aker is the earth understood as a passage rather than a surface. He is drawn as two lions seated back to back with the sun disc between them, or as a strip of land with a head at each end, and the two heads are named yesterday and tomorrow: the sun enters at the west, travels through the body of the earth all night, and leaves at the east. That makes him a doorway with a guard at both ends. He restrains the coils of Apep in the underworld and swallows the venom of anything that bites, and spells invoke him against snakes. The image of the double lion outlasted Egyptian religion, passing into later art as the pair of guardian lions flanking a gate.
entities.variantTraditions: Aker is sometimes pluralised into the Akeru, a group of earth-lions, and is closely related to Ruty, the double lion identified with Shu and Tefnut.

entities.name: Bata and Anpu
entities.role: The two brothers of the oldest surviving folk tale
entities.bio: Brothers of a Nineteenth Dynasty story: falsely accused, transformed repeatedly, and finally restored to the throne.
entities.longBio: The Tale of Two Brothers, on Papyrus D'Orbiney, is one of the oldest folk narratives to survive anywhere. Anpu's wife propositions his younger brother Bata; refused, she accuses him of assault, and Anpu waits with a knife. Warned by his cattle, Bata flees, proves his innocence by mutilating himself, and goes to the Valley of the Cedar, where he places his heart in a blossom at the top of a tree so that his life is stored outside his body. The gods make him a wife; she betrays him to the pharaoh and has the tree cut down, and Bata dies. Anpu searches years for the heart, finds it, and revives him. Bata then becomes a bull, is slaughtered; two persea trees spring from his blood, are cut down; a splinter enters his former wife's mouth and she bears him as her own son, who grows up to become king and to judge her.
entities.variantTraditions: The motif of the life hidden outside the body recurs across Eurasian folklore, and the opening episode has been compared with the Genesis account of Joseph and Potiphar's wife.

entities.name: Khufu
entities.role: The king of the Westcar Papyrus
entities.bio: Builder of the Great Pyramid, who in the Westcar Papyrus listens to his sons tell tales of magicians.
entities.longBio: Khufu is a historical Fourth Dynasty king, and almost nothing survives of him personally except the largest building of the ancient world and one tiny ivory statuette. What survives instead is a literary Khufu. The Westcar Papyrus frames a set of stories as entertainments told to a bored king by his sons: a wax crocodile that becomes a real one and takes an adulterer, a jewel retrieved from a lake by folding the water back, and the magician Djedi who can reattach a severed head and who prophesies that three kings not of Khufu's line will be born to the wife of a priest of Ra. Herodotus, writing two thousand years later, reports an Egyptian tradition that Khufu was a tyrant who closed the temples and forced the whole country to labour, a reputation that has no support in Egyptian sources.
entities.variantTraditions: Herodotus' hostile portrait is very late and probably reflects Late Period resentment of the pyramid age rather than any Old Kingdom memory.

entities.name: Djedi
entities.role: The magician of the Westcar Papyrus
entities.bio: A magician of a hundred and ten who reattaches severed heads and foretells the end of Khufu's line.
entities.longBio: Djedi is the last and most impressive of the magicians in the Westcar Papyrus, said to be a hundred and ten years old - the Egyptian ideal lifespan - and still eating five hundred loaves and drinking a hundred jugs of beer a day. Brought before Khufu, he is asked to demonstrate his reputed ability to reattach a severed head. A prisoner is offered; Djedi refuses flatly, saying it may not be done to a human being, and performs it instead on a goose, a waterbird and an ox. That refusal is the moral centre of the story and unusually explicit for Egyptian literature. He then delivers the prophecy Khufu actually wants: the secret chambers of Thoth will come to the eldest of three children about to be born to the wife of a priest of Ra, who will become kings after him.
entities.variantTraditions: The papyrus breaks off before the prophecy is fulfilled; the three children are presented as the first kings of the Fifth Dynasty.

entities.name: Sinuhe
entities.role: The exile who came home
entities.abode: Retjenu in the Levant, then Egypt
entities.bio: A court official who flees Egypt on the king's death, prospers abroad, and returns to be buried at home.
entities.longBio: The Story of Sinuhe is the most admired work of Egyptian literature and the one most often called a novel before novels. Overhearing news of Amenemhat I's assassination, Sinuhe panics for reasons the text never fully explains and flees, nearly dying of thirst before Bedouin rescue him. In Retjenu he marries a chief's daughter, becomes wealthy and powerful, and kills a champion who challenges him in single combat. Yet he cannot settle, because to die abroad is to be buried wrong, and the fear that grips him is not of death but of a foreign grave. Senusret I writes offering him return, and the reunion scene at court, where the royal children fail to recognise the sunburnt old man, is one of the finest things to survive from the ancient world. He is given a tomb, and the story ends with his shedding of the desert and reception of proper burial.
entities.variantTraditions: The historicity of Sinuhe is doubtful and largely beside the point; the text was copied for centuries as a model of fine writing.

entities.name: Horus the Elder
entities.role: The elder falcon; the sky whose eyes are sun and moon
domains: the sun and moon as his eyes
entities.bio: The older sky-falcon, brother of Osiris and Set, distinct from Horus the child of Isis.
entities.longBio: Egyptian religion carried at least two Horuses and never fully separated them. Haroeris is the elder: a sky god whose two eyes are the sun and the moon, born of Geb and Nut alongside Osiris, Isis, Set and Nephthys, and therefore Set's brother rather than his nephew. In this version the struggle between Horus and Set is a contest between brothers over the whole world, not a nephew's suit for his father's throne, and it is this older Horus who loses an eye to Set and has it healed. Later theology folded the two together, so that the same god is both Osiris' brother and his son, which the Egyptians tolerated without difficulty.
entities.variantTraditions: Kom Ombo's double temple honours Haroeris in one half and Sobek in the other; the merging of the two Horuses is never resolved in the sources.

entities.name: Montu
entities.role: Falcon god of war
domains: the strength of the king in combat
symbols: the falcon head with sun disc and two plumes
entities.bio: War god of the Theban region, whose name kings invoked when describing themselves in battle.
entities.longBio: Montu was the chief god of the Theban nome before Amun overtook him, and he kept a specific and vivid role afterwards: he is the fury of the king in battle. Mentuhotep II, who reunified Egypt after the First Intermediate Period, is named for him, and New Kingdom war annals describe the pharaoh raging among the enemy like Montu. He is falcon-headed like Horus but crowned with the sun disc and two tall plumes, and carries a curved khopesh sword. The white Buchis bull kept at Armant was his living manifestation, as Apis was Ptah's. The Greeks, reasonably enough, identified him with Ares.
entities.variantTraditions: Montu absorbed and was absorbed by several local falcon gods around Thebes, and appears fused as Montu-Ra and Montu-Horus.

entities.name: Onuris
entities.role: He who brings back the distant one
domains: the recovery of the Distant Goddess
entities.bio: Hunter god who brings the raging Distant Goddess home from Nubia.
entities.longBio: Onuris' name is a sentence: he who brings back the distant one. The Distant Goddess is the Eye of Ra in her furious form, withdrawn into Nubia as a lioness, and where Thoth talks her home Onuris hunts her down and brings her back with a lance and a rope, returning with her as his consort Mekhit. That makes him a god of the hunt and, because the same energy applies to enemies, of war; kings invoked him against foreigners. He is shown as a bearded man in a four-plumed crown, one arm raised to throw the spear, and he is one of the few major Egyptian gods depicted as fully human. The Greeks identified him with Ares.
entities.variantTraditions: The Distant Goddess he retrieves is called Mekhit, Tefnut or Hathor depending on the temple; each city preferred its own.

entities.name: Banebdjedet
entities.role: The ram of Mendes
domains: the union of the four great gods in one ba
entities.bio: Four-headed ram god who counsels caution in the tribunal of Horus and Set.
entities.longBio: The Egyptian word ba means both ram and soul, and Banebdjedet exploits the pun completely: he is the ram who is the ba, and his four heads are said to be the bas of Ra, Shu, Geb and Osiris gathered in one animal. In the Contendings of Horus and Set he plays the part of the cautious elder, advising the tribunal against a hasty verdict and proposing that Neith be consulted, which she is. His fertility aspect is emphatic and the living ram kept at Mendes was treated as his manifestation and buried in a granite sarcophagus. Herodotus reported rites at Mendes that later writers repeated with relish and which modern scholarship treats as a Greek misunderstanding.
entities.variantTraditions: Banebdjedet is sometimes conflated with the ram of Khnum at Elephantine, though the species and the theology differ.

entities.name: Satis
entities.role: Goddess of the cataract and the flood's arrival
symbols: the white crown with antelope horns
entities.bio: Guardian of Egypt's southern border who releases the flood and purifies the dead with cataract water.
entities.longBio: Satis stands at the frontier: her city Elephantine sat at the first cataract, the boundary between Egypt and Nubia, and she is both the archer who guards that border and the goddess who pours out the inundation from the caverns there. In the Pyramid Texts she purifies the dead king with four jars of water from the cataract, which is her funerary role. With Khnum and Anuket she forms the triad of the cataract region, generally as Khnum's consort. Her crown is unusual and memorable: the tall white crown of Upper Egypt flanked by a pair of antelope horns.
entities.variantTraditions: Satis is sometimes given as Khnum's daughter rather than consort, and her name is variously rendered Satet or Setet.

entities.name: Anuket
entities.role: Goddess of the cataract and the gazelle
symbols: a tall crown of reeds or feathers
entities.abode: Sehel Island, at the first cataract
entities.bio: Third of the cataract triad, whose name means the embracer - the flood clasping the fields.
entities.longBio: Anuket completes the Elephantine triad with Khnum and Satis, usually as their daughter. Her name comes from a verb meaning to embrace, and the sense is agricultural: the rising water clasps the fields and leaves them fertile. She is shown in a tall crown of reeds or plumes, and the gazelle is her animal, so she is sometimes called mistress of Nubia, where gazelles were common. Her island of Sehel carried a large sanctuary. At the height of the inundation her festival involved throwing coins, gold and jewellery into the river as thanks, and cowrie shells associated with her were worn as protective amulets by women.
entities.variantTraditions: In some periods Anuket takes on a more erotic character; her role shifts noticeably between the Middle and New Kingdoms.

entities.name: Ihy
entities.role: The sistrum player; child of Hathor
domains: the shaking of the sistrum in ritual
entities.bio: The child god who shakes the sistrum, embodying the joy of Hathor's music.
entities.longBio: Ihy is the son of Hathor and Horus of Edfu, and completes the Dendera triad. He is shown as a naked child with the sidelock of youth, a finger at his lips in the standard Egyptian gesture for a child, holding a sistrum - the rattle shaken in Hathor's rites, whose sound was believed to please the goddess and drive off hostility. His name has been read as sistrum player or as calf, both fitting a child of the cow goddess. He has essentially no narrative; his significance is that the rattling of the instrument in the temple is itself divine, so the sound of the ritual has a god of its own.
entities.variantTraditions: Ihy is sometimes identified with Harsomtus, another child of Hathor at Dendera, and the two are hard to separate.

entities.name: Heka
entities.role: Magic itself, personified
domains: the force that makes ritual effective
symbols: the raised arms of the ka sign
entities.abode: In the solar barque, and in every effective ritual
entities.bio: The power that makes magic and ritual work, present at creation before anything else was made.
entities.longBio: Heka is the energy that makes any ritual act effective, and Egyptians understood it as a natural force rather than a transgression - there is no Egyptian category of forbidden magic in the way later cultures developed. A Coffin Text has Heka declare that he came into being before duality existed, which places him prior even to the first division of the world, and he travels in the solar barque as part of its defence. Because healing was performed through spells as much as through drugs, physicians worked under him alongside Sekhmet and Serqet, and the standard Egyptian medical papyri mix pharmacology and incantation without any sense of a boundary. His emblem, two entwined serpents on a staff, resembles the later caduceus.
entities.variantTraditions: Heka is paired in some texts with Hu, authoritative utterance, and Sia, perception, as the three faculties by which Atum created.

entities.name: Hu and Sia
entities.role: Utterance and perception
domains: the faculties by which creation happened
symbols: a place in the solar barque
entities.abode: The solar barque, at Ra's side
entities.bio: The two faculties Atum used to create: the perception that conceives and the word that commands.
entities.longBio: Egyptian creation theology repeatedly separates thinking a thing from saying it, and personifies both. Sia is perception, the mind that conceives; Hu is the authoritative utterance, the word that makes what was conceived exist. Together with Heka, the force that makes the utterance effective, they are the machinery of creation by speech, which is the Memphite Theology's central claim about Ptah and appears in Heliopolitan texts about Atum as well. In the Pyramid Texts, Atum is said to have created them from drops of his own blood. They stand in the solar barque with Ra as permanent attendants, which is the tradition's way of saying that the sun's daily course is itself an act of intelligent speech rather than a mechanism.
entities.variantTraditions: Hu and Sia are usually treated as a pair; a third, Hehu, occasionally joins them, and their relation to Heka is stated differently in different texts.

entities.name: Sopdet
entities.role: The star Sirius, whose rising announced the flood
domains: the heliacal rising that opened the year
entities.abode: The eastern sky before dawn in midsummer
entities.bio: The goddess of Sirius, whose reappearance at dawn marked the new year and the imminent flood.
entities.longBio: Sirius disappears from the Egyptian sky for about seventy days each year and returns just before dawn in midsummer, within days of the Nile beginning to rise. Egyptians built their calendar on that coincidence: the heliacal rising of Sopdet opened the year, and the observation is precise enough that modern chronology of the whole ancient Near East partly depends on recorded sightings of it. She is shown as a woman with a five-pointed star above her head. With Sah, the constellation Orion identified with Osiris, she forms a celestial pair, and their child is Sopdu; the family is a sky version of Isis, Osiris and Horus, and Sopdet is regularly identified with Isis outright.
entities.variantTraditions: The 365-day civil calendar drifted against the true year by a day every four years, so the civil new year and Sopdet's rising coincided only once every 1,460 years - the Sothic cycle.

entities.name: Sah
entities.role: The constellation Orion
domains: the destination of the dead king
symbols: a star-covered figure holding a was sceptre
entities.bio: Orion personified, identified with Osiris, and the star-destination of the dead king.
entities.longBio: The Pyramid Texts send the dead king to the imperishable stars and specifically to Sah, and the identification of Orion with Osiris is one of the oldest in Egyptian religion, with Sopdet-Sirius as his consort trailing behind him across the sky. The constellation's disappearance and reappearance made it a natural figure for the god who dies and returns. Sah is shown striding, covered in stars, sometimes looking back over his shoulder toward Sopdet. The alignment of certain Old Kingdom pyramid shafts toward Orion has attracted an enormous amount of speculative literature; the association of the king with the constellation, however, is stated plainly in the texts themselves and needs no speculation.
entities.variantTraditions: The 'Orion correlation' theories about the Giza layout are not accepted by Egyptology; the textual link between the dead king and Sah is separate and secure.

entities.name: Mehet-Weret
entities.role: The great flood; the celestial cow
symbols: a cow lying on a reed mat
the sun disc between her horns
entities.bio: A cow goddess who is the water on which the sun sails and out of whom it was born.
entities.longBio: Mehet-Weret means the great flood, and she is the celestial water understood as a cow - Egyptians conceived the sky as a great expanse of water on which the solar barque sails, and she is that expanse. In one account the sun rose from between her horns at the first morning, making her the mother of Ra, and she is shown as a recumbent cow with the disc between her horns and a menat at her neck. She carries the newly born sun on her back. She is closely identified with Hathor, Neith and Nut, all of whom carry celestial-cow imagery, and it is often impossible to say which of them a given cow in a funerary papyrus is meant to be.
entities.variantTraditions: The Book of the Heavenly Cow describes the sky-cow lifting Ra away from mankind after the near-extermination; whether that cow is Mehet-Weret, Nut or Hathor is not resolved.

entities.name: Shezmu
entities.role: Lord of the oil press and of the slaughter block
entities.bio: God of the press: he makes perfume and unguents, and crushes the heads of the condemned in the same machine.
entities.longBio: Shezmu is a startling figure because the Egyptians declined to separate two things the press does. He operates the oil and wine press, and so he is the god of perfumed unguents, essential to both the living and the embalmed. He also operates it on the heads of the damned in the underworld, and Pyramid Text passages describe him pressing the enemies of the king and serving their blood as wine. The visual pun is exact and deliberate: red liquid comes out of the press either way. He has a benign aspect at Dendera and Edfu as the maker of sacred oils, and a terrifying one in the funerary texts, and both were maintained side by side without embarrassment.
entities.variantTraditions: His two aspects are so different that older scholarship assumed two gods; the press is the link, and the Egyptians clearly saw them as one.

entities.name: Babi
entities.role: The baboon of the underworld
domains: the guarding of the dark waters
entities.bio: A ferocious baboon god who feeds on entrails and whose phallus is the bolt of heaven's doors.
entities.longBio: Babi is the male hamadryas baboon at its most alarming - aggressive, territorial and conspicuously virile - and the Egyptians made a god of exactly that. He is said to feed on the entrails of the unjust dead, and spells in the Book of the Dead are directed at protecting the deceased from him. His virility is put to structural use: his phallus is described as the bolt on the doors of heaven and as the mast of the ferry that carries the dead across the underworld waters. Because of that association, spells invoke him to secure sexual potency in the afterlife. He stands in contrast to the other Egyptian baboon, the calm ibis-associated Thoth baboon of the moon.
entities.variantTraditions: The hamadryas baboon serves both Thoth and Babi in completely opposite registers, which is a good illustration of how Egyptian symbolism attaches to observed behaviour rather than to species.

entities.name: Imentet
entities.role: The goddess of the west
domains: the west as the land of the dead
the reception of the newly dead
symbols: the emblem of the west on her head
entities.abode: The western desert, at the edge of the cultivation
entities.bio: The personified West, who meets the newly dead at the desert edge and offers food and water.
entities.longBio: Egyptians buried on the west bank because the sun died there, and the west became a synonym for the realm of the dead; the dead themselves are called the westerners. Imentet is that direction personified, a woman wearing the hieroglyph for west on her head, and her role is a gentle one. She stands at the boundary between the cultivated land and the desert, sometimes emerging from the trunk of a sycamore, and offers bread and water to the newly arrived - the first hospitality of the afterlife. She frequently merges with Hathor as Mistress of the West and with Isis. The gesture of the goddess in the tree pouring water for the dead is one of the warmer images in Egyptian funerary art.
entities.variantTraditions: Imentet is rarely an independent figure and is usually an aspect of Hathor or Isis; her iconography is more distinct than her theology.

entities.name: Tatenen
entities.role: The risen land
symbols: the ram's horns and twin plumes
entities.bio: The primeval mound itself, personified: the first ground to rise from the water.
entities.longBio: Tatenen is the moment the land appears - the mound emerging from Nun on which creation becomes possible - held as a permanent god rather than a past event. His name means the risen land, and he is shown with green skin because he is the fertile earth, wearing a crown of ram's horns and tall plumes. Everything the earth contains falls to him, so he is the lord of quarries, mines and metal ores, which mattered greatly to a state that organised expeditions for stone and copper. At Memphis he was merged with Ptah as Ptah-Tatenen, giving the craftsman-creator a physical ground to stand on and to work with, and in that form he is invoked in royal texts as the father of the king.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Tatenen was originally independent of Ptah or always an aspect of him is unclear; the fused form dominates the surviving record.

entities.name: Mnevis
entities.role: The living bull of Ra at Heliopolis
domains: the living presence of the sun god
symbols: the sun disc and uraeus between the horns
entities.bio: A black bull kept at Heliopolis as the living manifestation of Ra, as Apis was of Ptah.
entities.longBio: Where Memphis had the Apis of Ptah, Heliopolis had the Mnevis of Ra: a living black bull housed at the temple, treated as the god's herald, consulted for oracles, and buried with full ceremony at death. Unlike the Apis, whose markings were minutely specified, the Mnevis was identified mainly by being wholly black with forward-growing hair. Its burials have been found at Heliopolis in stone-lined chambers. The bull cults show a strain of Egyptian religion quite different from the temple statue: the god is not represented, he is present, in an animal that eats and ages and dies and has to be replaced. Akhenaten, who abolished nearly everything, explicitly preserved the Mnevis, which says something about how deeply rooted it was.
entities.variantTraditions: The relationship between Mnevis, Apis and the Buchis bull of Armant was one of parallel local cults rather than a single system.

entities.name: Buchis
entities.role: The white bull of Montu
domains: the living presence of the war god
symbols: a white bull with a black face
entities.bio: A white bull with a black face kept at Armant as the living Montu, buried in the Bucheum.
entities.longBio: The Buchis is the third of the great Egyptian bull cults, the manifestation of the war god Montu at Armant. Its required marking was a white body with a black face, and ancient writers claimed its hair grew in the opposite direction to other cattle and that its colour changed hourly - the sort of detail that indicates a closely watched sacred animal accumulating lore. It was consulted as an oracle and had a reputation for healing. Its burials, in the underground gallery called the Bucheum, run from the Thirtieth Dynasty into the Roman period, and the dated stelae there are a useful chronological source. The cows that mothered the bulls were buried separately nearby.
entities.variantTraditions: The Bucheum stelae continue to 340 CE, making the Buchis one of the last documented Egyptian animal cults.
